The words

Hark! upon the morning breezes,
In the darkness, ere the waking,
Music sweet the senses pleases,
Soft upon the stillness breaking; —
"Glory, Glory!" this the singing,
Welcome to Immanuel bringing.

Shepherds at their watch beholding
Angels clad in glistening whiteness,
Heard the wondrous news unfolding
'Mid that dazzling scene of brightness; —
"Glory, Glory!" peace, and kindness,
Light is breaking on our blindness.

Glorious morn! The sun uprising,
Shone upon a world rejoicing;
God is with us, truth surprising;
List to song the message voicing, —
"Glory, Glory!" ages told it,
Heavenly voices now unfold it.

God adored, our nature wearing!
Ah, such condescending meekness!
Stooping to a world despairing,
Full of pity for our weakness; —
"Glory, Glory!" praises swelling,
God hath made with man His dwelling.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Ab and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (E♭), on the word “Hark”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 3/2 means three minim beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

John Brownlie translated these words from the Greek service books for Hymns from the Morningland (Paisley, 1911), headed “Christmas”.

The book printed the words without tunes. They are in Long Metre, six lines (8.8.8.8.8.8), and this page sets them to SELENA; any other Long Metre, six lines tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Traditional Greek
  • Translated (1911): John Brownlie (1857–1925)
  • Music (1850): Isaac B. Woodbury (1819–1858)

Tune SELENA by Isaac B. Woodbury (1819–1858); words by Traditional Greek; translated by John Brownlie (1857–1925).

Questions about Hark! upon the Morning Breezes

What is the doh of Hark! upon the Morning Breezes?

In this version, in Ab major, doh is Ab. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Hark! upon the Morning Breezes start on?

It starts on s (E♭ in Ab major), a pickup on the word “Hark” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is Hark! upon the Morning Breezes in the public domain?

Yes. John Brownlie died in 1925, Isaac B. Woodbury died in 1858; the words were in print by 1911 and the music in 1850. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
